planting.note: Grow in a container of chunky, well-draining aroid mix (bark, perlite, and coarse coir) under bright indirect light and high humidity; this recently introduced Ecuadorian species is strictly a tropical houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside frost-free climates. Water once the top layer of substrate dries, then water thoroughly. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Anthurium ivanportillae is a recently described Ecuadorian cloud-forest species named for aroid collector Ivan Portilla, grown for its long, dark green leaves marked with deep, parallel longitudinal ribbing that gives the whole blade a corrugated, almost pleated texture. Mature leaves develop a pronounced undulating, wavy margin as they lengthen, making this one of the more sculptural foliage anthuriums to enter cultivation in recent years. As an epiphyte from humid lower-montane forest, it wants bright filtered light rather than direct sun, chunky bark-based media that drains quickly, and relative humidity above 65 percent to size up its leaves properly. Keep night temperatures above 60F, since the species shows little cold tolerance and will stall or rot in cool, wet conditions.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden — Araceae collections and Anthurium cloud-forest species notes
International Aroid Society — new Anthurium species from Ecuador

planting.note: Grow in a container with a mossy pole or totem for climbing support, in bright indirect light and cool, humid conditions; this hemiepiphytic species is strictly a tropical houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside frost-free climates. Water when the top layer of growing medium dries. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Anthurium cutucuense is a vining, hemiepiphytic species from the cloud forests of the Cordillera de Cutucú in Ecuador, where young plants begin as single-leafleted seedlings on the forest floor before climbing into the canopy and transitioning to the trisected, deeply bullate adult leaf form with a contrasting red midrib. The strongly quilted, matte sub-velvety leaf segments make mature specimens a striking textural centerpiece distinct from the broad, heart-shaped velvet anthuriums more commonly grown. It prefers cooler nights than many tropical aroids — thriving with days in the 70s to low 80s F and nights dropping into the 50s and 60s — reflecting its mid-elevation Andean origin, so avoid hot, stagnant growing conditions. Provide a moss pole or similar support early so the plant can climb and mature into its distinctive trisect foliage rather than remaining in its juvenile single-leaf stage.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden — Araceae collections and Ecuadorian Anthurium species notes
International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List — Anthurium cutucuense assessment
Specialty aroid nursery cultivation sheets (Foliage Factory, Black Jungle Terrarium Supply) — Anthurium cutucuense care

planting.note: Mount or pot in a hanging basket with chunky, fast-draining aroid mix so the long leaves can hang freely; this epiphytic species is strictly a tropical houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside frost-free climates. Water when the top layer of substrate dries, and keep humidity high. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Anthurium pendulifolium is an epiphytic species from the wet lowland and foothill forests of Colombia, Ecuador, and northern Peru, named for its dramatically spreading-pendant leaves, which can stretch several feet in length on a mature plant. Unlike the broad, heart-shaped velvet anthuriums, it carries narrow, strap-like foliage that drapes downward, making it best suited to hanging baskets, mounted culture, or elevated shelving where the leaves have room to cascade. Give it bright but indirect light, since its native habitat at low to moderate elevation is shaded by taller canopy trees, and keep humidity consistently high to prevent the long leaf tips from browning. Because it is an epiphyte in nature, a chunky, open growing medium of bark and perlite that mimics tree-bark crevices works better than dense potting soil.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online, Anthurium pendulifolium
Missouri Botanical Garden — Araceae collections, pendent-leaf Anthurium species notes
Dave's Garden PlantFiles — Anthurium pendulifolium grower reports

common_name: Tomato Anthurium (Clidemioides Anthurium, Bullate Vining Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow under cover or in a terrarium/vivarium setup with very high humidity and a climbing support, since this species needs consistently wet-tropical conditions to thrive. Water when the top layer of growing medium dries but never let it go fully dry. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Anthurium clidemioides, nicknamed the Tomato Anthurium, is a climbing epiphyte native to the high-rainfall forests of Costa Rica, Panama, and Colombia, grown for its glossy, almost stalkless, strongly bullate leaves and showy red spathes. It is one of only two Anthurium species, along with A. flexile, that roots directly from the stem between leaf nodes as it climbs, an adaptation that lets it cling tightly to mossy bark in its wet-forest habitat. Because its origin areas receive exceptionally high year-round precipitation, it performs best under terrarium, vivarium, or greenhouse culture where humidity can be kept consistently elevated rather than in typical open-room houseplant conditions. Provide a damp, mossy climbing support and bright but filtered light to encourage the tightly clinging growth habit and reliable flowering seen in habitat.
sources: International Aroid Society — Anthurium species profile, A. clidemioides
Encyclopedia of Life — Anthurium clidemioides Standl.
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online, Anthurium clidemioides

planting.note: Grow in a container of chunky, well-draining aroid mix in partial to light shade; this compact heirloom pigtail anthurium is strictly a tropical houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside frost-free climates. Water when the top layer of growing medium dries. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Rothschildianum is a long-cultivated heirloom cultivar of the pigtail anthurium, Anthurium scherzerianum, distinguished from the plain red or orange-red species by a red spathe heavily speckled with white spots and set off by a curling yellow spadix. It is a compact, epiphytic plant native to Costa Rica, staying considerably smaller than the showier A. andraeanum flamingo flowers, with leaves typically under 8 inches, making it well suited to windowsills and small collector shelves. Like other scherzerianum selections it blooms young and repeatedly through the year, with each curiously speckled spathe lasting many weeks, though the flowers are too short-stemmed for cutting. Give it partial to light shade rather than deep shade, since flowering slows markedly in low light, and keep it warm and humid as befits its tropical epiphytic origin.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Anthurium scherzerianum 'Rothschildianum' plant profile
American Horticultural Society — A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants, Anthurium entries
Missouri Botanical Garden — Anthurium scherzerianum species and cultivar notes

planting.note: Grow in a container of chunky, well-draining aroid mix in bright indirect light or strong artificial light; this commercial Dutch-bred flamingo flower cultivar is strictly a tropical houseplant outside frost-free climates. Water when the top inch of growing medium dries, and avoid letting the pot stand in water. All parts are toxic if ingested.

directions: Pandola is a commercial Anthurium andraeanum cultivar from Dutch pot-plant breeding, notable among standard flamingo flowers for its two-tone spathe that blushes pink around a deeper green-tinged center rather than reading as a single solid color. The glossy, dark green, leathery heart-shaped leaves provide a dense backdrop that shows off the long-lasting blooms, each pale pink spadix remaining attractive for several weeks before fading. As with other florist-type andraeanum cultivars, it is bred for compact, even pot habit rather than garden vigor, so it performs best as a long-term container houseplant rather than a landscape subject in all but the warmest, most humid climates. Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the leaves, and maintain even moisture without waterlogging the roots to support continuous flowering.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Anthurium 'Pandola' plant profile
